name: Angkor Wat
label: Angkor Wat
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1113380295: large area 'Angkor Wat' (1440 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: The world's largest religious monument, famous for its sunrise reflection in the pond.

text.description:
Angkor Wat is the largest religious complex in the world, and it looks the part. A broad moat and an outer wall surround three raised galleries that climb towards a central group of five towers. The whole site covers about 162.6 hectares. It was built in the 12th century for the Khmer king Suryavarman II, first as a Hindu temple to Vishnu. Over the centuries it became a Buddhist temple and is still a place of worship today. Unusually for the temples around Angkor, it faces west.

It photographs well because of its scale and its order. The towers, galleries and moat repeat in clear lines, so even a quick phone shot has a strong shape. The walls also carry long bas-reliefs and carved figures called devatas, which reward a closer look.

Use that direction to build a wide view of the towers and galleries, then walk closer for details. The temple is huge, so decide first whether you want the whole building in one frame or a single carved wall. Trying to get both from one spot usually disappoints. Keep your phone lens clean, because dust and humidity can soften the picture. Take a few frames at each place, and step aside so other visitors can pass.
text.geographic_location: Angkor Wat stands in the Angkor area, in the Siem Reap region of Cambodia, inside the old Khmer capital of Angkor.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground, tram or railway stop to start from, so begin in Siem Reap town and plan your own way to Angkor Wat. Then follow the map to the phone icon on the map. From there the middle of the temple is about 156 m to the south-east, roughly 2 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 160 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit in the galleries, towers and moat at close range. Use the default lens (1x) for most views, as it looks most natural. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tops of the towers and for carved details on the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 160 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the towers or galleries with a horizontal line so the building does not lean. Leave some foreground, such as stonework or open ground, to show how big the place is. For carvings, move in close and shoot along the wall rather than straight on, to bring out the relief.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the stone to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Inside shaded galleries, tap the carvings and nudge the exposure up. Live Photos can catch passing monks or visitors, but ask before photographing people up close.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. Midday sun is harsh on pale stone and can make the shadows dark.

text.access_note: Angkor Wat is an active place of Buddhist worship, so check the official site before you go for current visiting rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning and late afternoon light is usually softer and the site is usually less crowded then.
Midday sun is harsh on pale stone and makes deep shadows.
Shaded galleries inside the temple are darker than the open areas outside.

name: Bayon
label: Bayon
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bayon (ប្រាសាទបាយ័ន)' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/6990223: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bayon' (168 m across).
notes: Temple known for its many giant smiling stone faces.

text.description:
The Bayon is the temple people picture when they think of stone faces. Towers rise in clusters, and each one has serene, smiling faces carved on every side. There are 216 of these faces, which many scholars read as portraits of King Jayavarman VII, the Buddhist king who built the temple in the late 12th or early 13th century. It stands at the very centre of his walled capital, Angkor Thom, and it was the last state temple built at Angkor.

It photographs well because the faces are everywhere and the towers are packed close together, so you can find a new angle every few steps. The outer gallery also has long bas-reliefs showing armies on the march, processions and scenes of everyday life, which make good detail shots.

For the best close-up on a phone, stand right at the base of one of the central face towers (the phone icon on the map) and shoot upwards. The faces then look huge, and the vertical lines lean in towards each other. If you can step back, the full towers against the sky make a calmer picture, and a second good spot is one that lets you line up three towers in a single frame in warm late sun.

The upper terrace, where many older guides took their nose-to-nose shots, is reported closed for restoration, so check what is open when you arrive. Go early or late in the day, when the sun comes in low and shows off the carving.
text.geographic_location: The Bayon is in the Angkor area near Siem Reap, at the exact centre of the walled city of Angkor Thom. Angkor Wat lies to the south of it.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or stops nearby, so go by taxi or hired scooter from Siem Reap town to Angkor Thom. Roads lead straight to the Bayon from the city's gates on the north, south, east and west sides. Ask your driver to drop you at the Bayon itself. From there, walk in to the base of a central face tower, which is the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) for the looking-up shot at the base of a tower. Use the default lens (1x) for whole towers against the sky. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for single faces and carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Looking up from here, you see a carved face with converging vertical lines and the huge scale of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Tilt the phone up and keep the face in the middle of the frame. Switch on gridlines so you can see how steeply the lines lean in. If you want a calmer view, step back and use the default lens (1x) to fit the full towers against the sky. Another good alternative is a spot where three towers line up in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the face to focus. Then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the stone. Take a second shot with the telephoto for detail, as the ultra-wide can stretch the edges of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when low side light brings out the carvings.

text.access_note: The Bayon is part of the Angkor complex and is still a Buddhist sanctuary, so check the official site before you go for tickets, opening times, dress expectations and which terraces are open.

name: Pub Street
label: Pub Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pub Street' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM N5816883154 (pub street): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Lively street of bars and restaurants, glowing at night.

text.description:
Pub Street is the lane of bars and restaurants in Siem Reap that is busiest after dark. Its official name is Street 08. The best photo is at the arch end, where an arch over the street glows with pink and blue lights and frames the bright lane of bars and people beyond it. The sign and arch are the most recognisable backdrop on the street.

It photographs best at night, once the neon is on. One local photographer says the arch looks strongest on a wet night, when the lights are reflected in the pavement. If it rains, wait for the shower to ease and shoot while the ground is still shiny.

Expect crowds and stalls along the street, and they can block the view. Be patient and wait for a gap, or shoot at a slight angle rather than straight on. If you want a wider, higher view, El Toro looks down the busy street with bars, lights and crowds below. You will need to buy a drink or a meal there, so check with the venue before you go.

Keep your phone steady, tuck your elbows in, and take a few frames so that at least one is sharp. Photograph the street as a whole rather than close-ups of strangers, which is friendlier and gives a better picture.
text.geographic_location: Pub Street (Street 08) is in Siem Reap.
text.directions_text: Find Pub Street (also called Street 08) in Siem Reap using a map app. Once you are on the street, walk to the arch end, which is the phone icon on the map shown on the map. No station or tram stop serves it, so check a map app for the route. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole arch and the lit street into one frame. The default lens (1x) gives a more natural look and usually copes better with low light. Telephoto (2x-5x) can pick out the arch lights or a distant stretch of street, but it often struggles in the dark.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the arch with its pink and blue lights frames the lit lane of bars and crowds. For the wider, higher view down the street, try El Toro as a second option.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the arch in the upper part of the frame, with the street running away below it. Keep the phone level so the sides of the street do not lean. After rain, crouch a little and hold the phone low to catch the reflections in the pavement. Wait for a gap in the crowd, or let a few people walk through the frame to give a sense of scale and life.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Use night mode if your phone offers it and hold still for the full exposure. Tap on the arch to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the neon colours stay rich rather than turning white. A Live Photo can help you pick the sharpest moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the neon is on. A rainy night is worth it if you want the reflections, as one local account recommends.

text.access_note: Pub Street is an open public street; the elevated view from El Toro needs a drink or meal purchase, so check with the venue before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Pub Street is the busiest lane in Siem Reap after dark.
The street is open to the public and does not need a ticket.
Night mode on most recent phones needs a steady hold for a second or more.
Lowering the exposure slider helps stop bright neon lights from washing out to white.
Shooting from a low position can show more of the reflections on a wet pavement.

name: Angkor Thom
label: Angkor Thom South Gate
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Tonle Om Gate' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Khloung Thvear Tonle Om' (way/471873115): middle (32 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1221842998: large area 'Angkor Thom' (4738 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Walled royal city entered over a causeway lined with statues.

text.description: Angkor Thom, the 'Great City', was the last and longest-lasting capital of the Khmer Empire, founded in the late twelfth century by King Jayavarman VII. Its walls are 8 m high and 3 km long on each side, and a moat runs around them. The best phone photo here is the south entrance, Tonle Om Gate. A tower about 23 m high, carved with large calm faces, stands at the end of a stone causeway. Rows of figures line the causeway, gods (devas) on the left and demons (asuras) on the right, each row holding a serpent as if in a tug-of-war. This is a scene from the Churning of the Sea of Milk myth. The gate is the main way into the city for visitors, so it is busy, but the long straight lines of the causeway make a tidy, balanced picture. If the moat is still, the gate may reflect in it. Come in early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and there are fewer tuk-tuks and groups. Vehicles use the causeway, so keep an eye out while you line up your shot. If you have time, Victory Gate and the North Gate are good alternatives, with trees growing around the carved faces.
text.geographic_location: Angkor Thom is inside the Angkor Archaeological Park, north of Angkor Wat and about 7 km north of Siem Reap town. Tonle Om Gate is its south entrance, about 1.7 km north of the Angkor Wat entrance.
text.directions_text: Travel north from central Siem Reap towards the Angkor temples; the journey takes around 30 minutes. The south gate is about 1.7 km north of the Angkor Wat entrance. Ask for 'Angkor Thom south gate' or 'Tonle Om'. Get out before the bridge and walk to the side of the causeway. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the moat, causeway, statues and gate tower in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view of the gate. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved faces on the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (on the causeway in front of the gate, standing on either side of the bridge over the moat). The gate tower with its giant faces at the end of a long causeway lined with gods and demons, often with the moat reflecting the scene. On either side of the bridge over the moat. The wider city of Angkor Thom stretches away to the north behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the causeway in the middle so the rows of statues lead to the gate. Crouch a little to bring the moat into the bottom of the frame and catch any reflection. Keep the tower upright, because tilting makes it lean. For a different view, Victory Gate gives a high angle down onto tuk-tuks passing under the gate, and the North Gate (Dei Chhnang Gate) shows its carved faces among trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the gate's faces to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the stone keeps its detail. Take a few frames in case a tuk-tuk or tour group walks through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and there are fewer tuk-tuks and groups.

text.access_note: Angkor Thom is inside the Angkor Archaeological Park, so you need an Angkor pass; check the official site before you go for current rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Reflections in the moat show best when the water is calm.
The ultra-wide lens can stretch statues and the tower near the edges of the frame, so keep the gate near the centre.
Crouching slightly lowers the viewpoint and brings more of the moat into the frame.

name: Ta Prohm
label: Ta Prohm
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ta Prohm' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/6987298: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ta Prohm' (480 m across).
notes: Temple swallowed by giant silk-cotton tree roots.

text.description:
Ta Prohm is the temple where huge trees have grown straight out of the stonework, and that is exactly why it photographs so well. King Jayavarman VII founded it in 1186 as a monastery dedicated to his mother, and most of it was built in the late 12th and early 13th centuries. The stones were laid without mortar, so once the place was abandoned, trees took root in the loosened stones. Conservation work in the 20th century deliberately left much of it looking as it was found. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1992.

This spot is at the northwest corner of the East Gate, the entry tower of the fourth enclosure. Spung tree roots spill over the corner of the gate, with the entry tower rising behind them. One photographer's guide calls it the most photographed spung tree in the temple, alongside the Tomb Raider Tree. The temple is often called the Tomb Raider Temple because of its part in the 2001 film.

A timber posing platform can end up in the frame, so shoot from above it, or go early, to keep people out of the picture. Stay on the marked wooden paths. Other good root-and-doorway scenes are inside the temple, so leave time to wander.
text.geographic_location: Ta Prohm is in the Angkor area just outside Siem Reap, about one kilometre east of Angkor Thom and on the southern edge of the East Baray. This spot is at the East Gate, the entry on the eastern side of the temple.
text.directions_text: Ta Prohm is near Siem Reap, about one kilometre east of Angkor Thom. Today visitors can only enter from the east or west side, so head for the East Gate if you want this spot. At the East Gate (the entry gopura of the fourth enclosure), look for its northwest corner, where the roots spill over the stonework. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the roots and the gate tower together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and want the whole root mass plus the tower. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out root details and to crop tighter if the platform or other visitors are in the way.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand at Ta Prohm, at the northwest corner of the East Gate (the entry tower of the fourth enclosure). From here the photo shows spung tree roots spilling over the corner of the gate, with the entry tower visible behind them. Stand a little above the timber posing platform if you can, so it stays out of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the roots in the foreground and the entry tower behind them, and turn on your gridlines to keep the tower upright. Keep the phone level so the stonework does not lean. If you want a quieter alternative, the stone doorway almost fully wrapped in silk-cotton tree roots, the classic Tomb Raider view, is elsewhere in the temple. Crowds are heavy there, and where exactly it sits is disputed, so check on the ground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the roots to set focus and exposure, then drag the exposure slider down a touch if the sky behind the tower is washing out. Check the frame for people or the platform before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when few people are around, according to a photographer's guide to the temple.

text.access_note: Ta Prohm is inside Angkor Archaeological Park, so entry needs an Angkor pass; check the official site before you go for current rules and opening times, and stay on the marked wooden paths.
claims_not_in_sources: The roots and the entry tower will look more even and less contrasty in shade or soft light, so the sky behind the tower may be bright and need the exposure slider.

name: Preah Khan
label: Preah Khan
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Preah Khan' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3046217: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Preah Khan' (311 m across).
notes: Long corridors with trees growing over the ruins.

text.description: Preah Khan, whose name means "Royal Sword", is a 12th-century Buddhist temple built for King Jayavarman VII in honour of his father. It was once far more than a temple. It worked as a city, a temple and a Buddhist university all in one. Today it is mostly left as it was found, with big trees growing through the stonework and fallen blocks lying in the passages. That gives you plenty of texture for photos. The temple faces east, so the east gate is the traditional main entrance. It is also the best place to start. Stand back from the gate and the stone doorway frames a single carved yoni (a stone base) in the foreground, with a line of repeating doorways behind it. Your eye is drawn straight through the temple. Coming in from the east side is also a quieter approach than the western entrance. Elsewhere on the site, the long causeway lined with guardian figures makes a good leading-line shot. Inside, the Hall of Dancers has apsara carvings on its walls and pillars, lit by light from the windows. The outer wall measures about 800 by 700 m, so allow time to wander. Keep your phone steady against a wall or pillar in the dim passages, and watch your footing on uneven stone.
text.geographic_location: Preah Khan is at Angkor, northeast of Angkor Thom and just west of the Jayatataka baray, the large reservoir beside it. It sits in the Angkor temple area, close to Neak Pean and Ta Prohm.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stops are listed for this spot, so you will need to arrange your own transport. Ask your driver for Preah Khan, which lies to the northeast of Angkor Thom. The temple is just west of the Jayatataka baray. Once there, head to the east gate and stand back from it for the first photo. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the east gate, so the doorway frames the scene naturally. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the long causeway or tight passages. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for carvings and the repeating doorways.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there, walk to the east gate (east gopura) and step back from it. From that spot the photo shows the east gate framed by its doorway, with the single yoni in the foreground and the repeating doorways behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the yoni low in the frame, with the doorways leading the eye into the temple. Keep the phone level so the stone arches don't lean. For a different view, shoot along the causeway with its guardian figures towards the entrance gate. Inside, the Hall of Dancers is good for apsara carvings in window light.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the doorway to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky doesn't wash out the stone. In dim passages, hold still and let night mode work if your phone offers it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually means softer light and fewer people. Check the official site for opening times before you go.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed site covered by the Angkor Pass, so check the official site before you go for opening hours and current rules.

name: Pre Rup
label: Pre Rup
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pre Rup' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/228275782: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Pre Rup' (206 m across).
notes: Red-brick temple mountain popular at sunset.

text.description:
Pre Rup is a Hindu temple built as the state temple of the Khmer king Rajendravarman and dedicated in 961 or early 962. It is a stepped 'temple mountain' of brick, laterite and sandstone. The pyramid rises in three steep tiers, and on top five towers stand in a pattern: one at each corner and one in the middle. The name means 'turn the body', and it comes from a popular belief that funerals were once held here.

It photographs well because of its colour. The laterite and brick give it a reddish tone that glows in early morning and late afternoon light. The phone icon on the map is on the west edge of the upper terrace. From there you look out over the rice fields, and at sunset the Angkor Wat towers line up on the western horizon. Guides describe the upper platform as a top sunset vantage.

The upper levels have steep stairs, and one guide says there are no railings, so take your time and keep a hand free. Arrive early enough to find a spot on the terrace before the light turns. If you would rather stay low, the sun can be framed between the two front towers from ground level. For a sunrise shot, the eastern face and central tower catch the first light.
text.geographic_location: Pre Rup is inside the Angkor Archaeological Park, just south of the East Baray (the old eastern reservoir). It lines up north to south with the East Mebon temple.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops here, so start from Siem Reap town and arrange a driver to take you to Pre Rup, just south of the East Baray. Ask your driver to wait or to come back for you, as the park is large. Once you are at the temple, climb to the upper terrace and walk to its west edge to reach the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the wide view across the rice fields. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the distant Angkor Wat towers closer. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) from ground level to fit all five towers into the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on Pre Rup, at the west edge of the upper terrace. From here you look west over the rice fields, with the Angkor Wat towers lined up on the western horizon at sunset.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon level, with the rice fields along the bottom third and the sky above. Let the line of towers sit just off-centre. If the terrace is busy, a short zoom can leave out other people. As an alternative, go back to ground level and shoot with the sun setting between the two front towers, with no climbing needed.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky near the sun to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the colours stay rich and the sky does not wash out. Take a few shots, as people move about on the terrace.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into sunset, roughly the last hour or two of daylight. Sunrise also works for the eastern face, lit warm against the morning sky.

text.access_note: Pre Rup is inside the Angkor Archaeological Park, which needs an Angkor pass, and opening hours vary between listings, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Siem Reap town is the usual starting point for reaching Pre Rup.
A driver can generally be arranged from Siem Reap town for getting to the temple.
The Angkor Wat towers look small on the horizon, so a telephoto lens helps bring them closer.
Lowering the exposure slider near a bright sunset sky generally keeps colours richer on a phone.

name: Phnom Bakheng
label: Phnom Bakheng
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Phnom Bakheng' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/228284686: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Phnom Bakheng' (246 m across).
notes: Hilltop temple, a classic sunset spot over Angkor Wat.

text.description: Phnom Bakheng is a hill temple at Angkor, built at the end of the 9th century in the reign of King Yasovarman (889–910). It rises about 65 m above the plain as a seven-level pyramid, with five sandstone sanctuaries on the top level. Most of the 108 small towers that once surrounded it have collapsed, but the stepped shape and weathered stonework still give you plenty to photograph. Most visitors climb up for the sunset view of Angkor Wat across the jungle, about 1.5 km to the southeast. This map suggests a quieter option. The phone icon on the map is on the northern terrace of the upper tiers, where the last low sun picks out carvings and stone textures. You get a close-up of the temple itself rather than the Angkor Wat skyline. If you want the skyline too, the view from the summit shows Angkor Wat's towers in the distance with the sun setting behind them. Use the telephoto lens for that shot, and expect the towers to look small. Numbers at the summit are limited, and one guide says the sunset lookout can fill by 5 pm, so arrive early. The steps are steep and there is no lighting after closing, so plan to leave soon after sunset.
text.geographic_location: Phnom Bakheng stands on a hill within the Angkor area, in Siem Reap Province. Angkor Wat lies about 1.5 km to the southeast.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station stops apply here, so start from Siem Reap town and travel to the foot of the Phnom Bakheng hill at Angkor. From there you climb the hill on foot to the upper tiers. The steps are steep, so allow extra time, especially in fading light. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for carvings and stonework on the northern terrace, and the telephoto (2x-5x) to pick out single details or, from the summit, the distant towers of Angkor Wat. The ultra-wide (0.5x) helps if you want to fit a whole terrace and its sanctuaries into one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on Phnom Bakheng, on the northern terrace of the upper tiers. From here the photo shows the temple's carvings and stonework lit by the last low sun, a close-up of the hill temple rather than the Angkor Wat skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up a carved panel or a sanctuary wall along one of them, with some terrace stone in the foreground for depth. For the alternative view, go to the summit, where Angkor Wat's towers appear in the distance across the jungle with the sun setting behind them. Zoom in with the telephoto and keep the treeline at the bottom of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the warm light stays rich and the sky does not wash out. Keep the phone steady against a wall or your body in dim light, and try night mode only if the light fades quickly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the low sun rays light the carvings. Aim to be in place well before sunset and head down soon afterwards.

text.access_note: Entry to Angkor needs an Angkor pass, and summit visitor numbers are limited, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Siem Reap town is a sensible place to start the journey.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) can fit a whole terrace with its sanctuaries into one frame.
Lowering the exposure slider slightly helps keep sunset colours and sky detail in this kind of light.
Night mode may help if the light fades quickly, but needs the phone held steady.

name: Angkor National Museum
label: Angkor Natl Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/322700733: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Angkor National Museum' (179 m across).
notes: Museum of Khmer history and Angkor artefacts.

text.description:
The Angkor National Museum is a large archaeological museum in Siem Reap. It opened on 12 November 2007 and tells the story of the Khmer Empire's Angkor period, roughly the 9th to 14th centuries, across eight galleries. Many of the objects were found in and around the Angkor sites nearby. Themes include the Gallery of 1,000 Buddha, the great Khmer kings, Angkor Wat and Angkor Thom, stone inscriptions, and ancient costume with apsara dancers.

For a phone photographer, the museum is mainly a building and entrance shot. It is a big, broad structure, so the outside is easiest to capture with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) from a little way back. A shot of the entrance with a few visitors walking in also gives a sense of scale and place. If you go inside, you will find themed galleries that follow a single flowing route, which keeps your photo walk simple. Photography rules inside can differ from room to room, so look for signs and check the official site before you go.

A sensible plan is to take your exterior photos on arrival, put the phone away for the galleries, then take a few last photos of anything you are allowed to capture. Wipe your lens first, as humid air and fingerprints can soften pictures.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in the town of Siem Reap, Cambodia, within reach of the Angkor archaeological sites whose finds it displays.
text.directions_text: There are no rail or tram links in the data for this spot. Ask a local driver or use a ride service to reach the Angkor National Museum in Siem Reap, and give the name of the museum. The phone icon on the map is at the museum itself, so you can start photographing as soon as you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole building in from a distance. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the entrance, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for architectural details or signs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Step back from the entrance until the whole front fits your screen, rather than shooting from right beside the doors.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the building's horizontal lines level with them. Hold the phone upright and level to avoid leaning walls. Include a few people near the entrance to show how big the building is.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building on screen to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the walls keep their detail. Wipe the lens before you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the front of a building than the middle of the day. If it is very hot and bright, look for even light and use the exposure slider.

text.access_note: This is a museum, so it is likely to be ticketed and to have set opening times and photography rules inside; check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The building is large and best captured from some distance with an ultra-wide lens.
There is open space in front of the entrance where you can step back to photograph the building.
Photography rules inside museums can differ between rooms or displays.
Morning or late afternoon light is usually softer than midday light.
Humid air and fingerprints can soften phone photos.

name: Terrace of the Elephants
label: Terrace of Elephants
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Terrace of the Leper King' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Terrace of the Leper King East Entrance' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/10928315: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Terrace of the Elephants' (335 m across).
notes: Long wall carved with life-size elephants.

text.description:
The Terrace of the Elephants is a long raised wall inside the walled city of Angkor Thom. The Royal Square is where its scale shows best. King Jayavarman VII used it as a platform to watch his army return in triumph, and it also served as a base for the king's grand audience hall. The wall is about 350 metres long. Its middle section carries life-size garudas and lions, and towards each end are the famous parades of elephants with their Khmer mahouts. It is named for the elephants carved on its eastern face.

The northern platform near the entrance, with the five-headed horse, is popular but very crowded, while the Leper King end is quieter. It suits close, unhurried pictures of weathered, sunken sculptures and the broken lines of old figures. From here you can also walk south along the wall in a few minutes to try the elephant carvings close up. If you want the whole length in one frame, the Royal Square, across from the wall, is the better spot, though it can be busy with wedding photo shoots in the late afternoon. Take a few detail shots first, then a wider one to show the wall rising above you.
text.geographic_location: Inside the walled city of Angkor Thom. It lies beside the Royal Square, next to the Terrace of the Leper King.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop here. Head for the Royal Square inside Angkor Thom. Once inside the walled city, head for the Royal Square and the long terrace beside it. From there, the middle of the terrace is about 3 minutes on foot to the south. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the sculptures on the Terrace of the Leper King. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for tight details of worn faces and carved lines. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you step back to show the length of the wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Terrace of the Leper King (north end of the Terrace of the Elephants, where it meets the Leper King terrace). Weathered, sunken sculptures and abstract lines of broken figures, shot as detail images. At the north end of the Terrace of the Elephants where the two meet. From here the photo shows weathered, sunken sculptures and the abstract lines of broken figures, shot as detail images. The long elephant wall runs away to the south. If you want the full length of the elephant reliefs, the garudas and the upper platform in one frame, try the Royal Square as an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Fill the frame with one section of carving rather than trying to catch everything. Turn on gridlines and line up the wall edge or a row of figures with a grid line. Take a closer shot of a single carving, then a wider one to show where it sits. For the elephants themselves, go to the terrace wall and shoot upwards so the wall rises above you.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the carving to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the stone keeps its texture and the sky does not turn white. Use the 2x-5x lens rather than pinching to zoom, and hold the phone steady against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the light on the day. Going earlier or later than the middle of the day usually helps the carvings. Late afternoon can be busy with wedding photo shoots on the Royal Square.

text.access_note: This is part of the Angkor Thom temple complex, so entry may be ticketed or restricted: check the official site before you go.

name: Banteay Kdei
label: Banteay Kdei
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Srah Srang' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Srah Srang' (way/568211774): middle (47 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3045422: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline '' (113 m across).
notes: Quiet monastery-style temple with Buddha-lined corridors.

text.description:
Banteay Kdei is a Buddhist temple from the mid-12th to early 13th century, built under Jayavarman VII in the Bayon style. It is similar in plan to Ta Prohm and Preah Khan but smaller and simpler. Its east gate has a cross-shaped plan with carved faces of Lokesvara, and the whole complex sits inside a long outer wall of about 700 m by 300 m. Monks lived here on and off until the 1960s, and restoration work is still going on.

A classic sunrise view is from the Srah Srang terrace across the water. From there you look west over the water to the temple's east gate and its long sandstone enclosure. The basin in the foreground gives the picture depth, and the temple sits low and calm along the far side. Guides often name this terrace as one of the better sunrise spots at Angkor, and it is usually less busy than Angkor Wat at that hour. Crowds are never guaranteed, though.

Start with the whole scene, then zoom in on the gate and the line of the wall. Some towers and corridors are restored or roped off, so the exact view may be partly blocked. If someone offers to guide you or show you photo spots, agree a price first or politely decline.
text.geographic_location: Banteay Kdei is in the Angkor Archaeological Park, south-east of Ta Prohm and east of Angkor Thom, directly opposite the Srah Srang reservoir.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground or tram stops here, so go from Siem Reap town by taxi or hired scooter and ask for Srah Srang, in the eastern part of the Angkor park. From the terrace, the temple's east gate lies to the west across the water, roughly 500 m away. Bring your Angkor pass, because it covers the temple. The terrace itself is outside the temple. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene: water, gate and wall together. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the gate and the line of the enclosure across the basin.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Srah Srang (east edge of the basin, facing the temple's east gate). Banteay Kdei's east gate and long sandstone enclosure across the water, with the basin in the foreground, typically framed at sunrise. At the east edge of the basin, and face west across the water towards the temple's east gate. From here the photo shows the long sandstone enclosure with the basin in front of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the lower third line, so the water fills the foreground and the temple sits along the upper line. Include a little of the terrace edge for scale. If you have time, the temple itself offers other views: the east approach with its lion statues and naga balustrades, and the outer south side with trees and stone walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the gate to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Take a few shots, because the light changes quickly at sunrise.

text.access_note: The temple is part of the Angkor park and is covered by the Angkor pass; the Srah Srang terrace is outside the temple, but check the official site before you go for current access.
claims_not_in_sources: From the east edge of the basin, the sun rises behind the photographer and lights the temple's east face (the east gate faces east, so this is likely but should be checked).
Calm water in the early morning can give a clearer reflection of the temple.
Exposure can be dimmed by tapping and dragging the slider; sunrise light changes quickly.

name: Baphuon
label: Baphuon
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Baphuon' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/240141751: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Baphuon temple' (106 m across).
notes: Three-tiered temple mountain in Angkor Thom.

text.description:
The Baphuon is a three-tiered temple mountain at Angkor, built in the mid-11th century as the state temple of Suryavarman I and first dedicated to Shiva. It later became a Buddhist temple. It is large, about 120 metres east to west and 100 metres north to south at its base, and it stands roughly 34 metres tall without its lost tower. That scale makes it a good subject even on a phone.

Most visitors photograph the long approach from the east. The more unusual picture is from the west side, where a reclining Buddha, about 9 metres tall and 70 metres long, was fitted into the second level. It was added in the 15th century according to recent carbon dating, though older estimates say the 16th century. It is not a statue you can simply see. It is an outline in the stonework, so it helps to stand back on the open ground and look at the whole wall. The temple also has a dramatic story. Its collapsed stones were left in numbered blocks when work stopped in 1970, and it was finally reopened in 2011 after a very long restoration.

Take a few frames from different distances. Start wide to show the whole pyramid, then zoom in on the carved lines of the Buddha. If you climb to the upper terrace for views over the treetops, expect a steep climb. Allow time, because access to the upper areas can close in the late afternoon.
text.geographic_location: The Baphuon is inside Angkor Thom, in the Angkor Archaeological Park north of Siem Reap town. It lies northwest of the Bayon and next to the southern edge of the old royal palace enclosure.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stops serve this spot. The Baphuon is inside Angkor Thom, in the Angkor Archaeological Park. Once inside Angkor Thom, the Baphuon lies northwest of the Bayon. A raised causeway leads up to the temple's eastern face. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) on the open ground to fit the whole western wall in the frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a natural view. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the carved outline of the reclining Buddha and the stone textures.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Walk to the open ground on the Baphuon's west side, face the temple and stand back there, where the outline of the reclining Buddha is visible. From there the large carved figure fills most of that side of the pyramid.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and keep the horizon level so the stepped stone tiers look straight. Place the Buddha's outline along one of the lines. As an alternative, shoot the long raised causeway on its columns from the eastern approach, with the pyramid rising behind it. Panorama mode also suits the causeway view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out the carving. If the Buddha outline looks faint, try a telephoto frame that fills the screen with the wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Afternoon is suggested for the western side, but check how the light looks on the day. Upper areas may close in the late afternoon.

text.access_note: The Baphuon is inside Angkor Thom, so you need an Angkor Archaeological Park pass; check the official site before you go for current access rules and any limits on the upper terrace.

name: Neak Pean
label: Neak Pean
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Neak Pean' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1066013: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Small island temple in a square pool.

text.description:
Neak Pean is a small temple on a circular island in the middle of a man-made pool, set in the old reservoir known as Jayatataka Baray. Its name means "the entwined serpents", after the carved snakes (nagas) that wind around the base of the island. That gives you something distinctive to photograph, as the carved tails make strong curved lines against the water.

The temple was built in the reign of King Jayavarman VII and is linked to Preah Khan. It was designed with healing in mind: four smaller pools around the central one stand for water, earth, fire and wind, each joined to the middle by a stone channel. The channels are shaped like the heads of animals (an elephant, a horse and a lion, with a human head on the east side). A statue of a horse, Balaha, is the only one of the original sculptures still standing in the water.

Visitors cannot go onto the central island, but a circular wooden platform runs around it. From there you can get close to the central tower and the carved serpent tails. A long wooden causeway leads to the platform, and the view along it, with the water and bare trees on either side, makes a good wider shot. Part of the site may be under renovation, so scaffolding can appear in some frames; try a different angle if it does. Water levels change through the year, so the pool may look empty and muddy in the dry season and give fuller reflections in the wet season.
text.geographic_location: Neak Pean lies in the Angkor area, near Siem Reap, in the old Jayatataka reservoir, which is associated with Preah Khan.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stops serve this spot, so plan your own route to the Angkor area. Neak Pean sits in the Jayatataka Baray, which is associated with Preah Khan, though I can't give a route. The causeway starts at the edge of the old reservoir, and the phone icon on the map is on the platform around the island at the end of it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) on the platform for the island and tower. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the long causeway view, and the telephoto (2x-5x) for the carved nagas and the central tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you get close-up views of the central tower and the carved naga tails at the base of the island, seen from the platform rather than from the island itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the gridlines to keep the tower upright, and place the carved tails along the lower third. For a wider shot, take a second photo from the wooden causeway, with the island at the end of it and the water and dead trees in front. The wider, quieter views across the reservoir toward the island are another option, with water plants in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the stonework keeps its detail. If the water is still, take a couple of shots to catch the reflection.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The wet season gives full reflections in the pool, while the dry season leaves it empty and muddy. Go in the early morning or late afternoon for softer light and fewer people.

text.access_note: The island itself is closed to visitors and the Angkor Pass is needed for entry, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer visitors.
Tapping to focus and lowering the exposure helps keep detail in stonework against a bright sky.
Still water may give a reflection of the island in the wet season.

name: Old Market (Siem Reap)
label: Old Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Old Market Bridge' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Old Market Bridge' (way/191526735): middle (35 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/42672882: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Old Market' (169 m across).
notes: Central market for souvenirs, food and local life.

text.description:
Old Market, known in Khmer as Phsar Chas, is a market in the south of Siem Reap. It is used by locals and visitors alike, and it is such a fixture that many businesses give their address in relation to it. Souvenir stalls sell silk, silverware, T-shirts, and wood and stone carvings. The food area has rice, dried fish, pork sausages, fruit, vegetables and baguettes.

This spot works because you can see the whole roofed market building from across the Siem Reap River. From the bridge, the water sits in the foreground and the market fills the middle of the frame. That gives you a calm scene-setting shot before you head into the busy aisles. The bridge also links the market with the Art Market, so it is easy to add to a walk.

Start on the east-bank approach to Old Market Bridge. Take a wide shot of the river and market, then walk on to Pokambor Avenue for a straight-on view of the outer frontage and roofline. If you go inside, the aisles are narrow and crowded, so keep your phone close and ask before photographing vendors up close. Conditions may have changed, so check on the day.
text.geographic_location: Old Market stands in the south part of central Siem Reap, on the opposite bank of the Siem Reap River from the Old Market Bridge approach. Many local businesses use it as a landmark for their address.
text.directions_text: No stations or tram stops are nearby; check local transport options to reach Old Market Bridge in central Siem Reap. Cross the river by the bridge to reach the market itself; it is a short walk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the main river-and-market view. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the roofline is cut off or you want more of the water. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for market details across the river.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Old Market Bridge (east bank approach, looking west across the Siem Reap River to the market). The roofed market building sits across the river from the bridge, so the frame includes the water in the foreground with the market beyond it. The roofed market building lies on the far bank, so the water fills the foreground with the market beyond it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the water along the lower third, with the market roofline across the middle. Keep the phone level so the building does not lean. For a different angle, try Pokambor Avenue for a straight-on view of the outer frontage, or go into the food area for close-ups of vendors and produce, asking permission first.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the market building to focus, then pull the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the roofs and water keep their detail. Take a Live Photo if people or traffic are moving, so you can pick the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the water, and the market is a livelier subject during the day. Try a quick shot at each end of the day and compare.

text.access_note: The bridge approach is an ordinary public place and the market is a busy working market; check the official site or locally before you go for current conditions and trading times.

name: Ta Keo
label: Ta Keo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Prasat Ta Keo' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/228152964: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ta Keo' (306 m across).

text.description: Ta Keo is a big, plain sandstone temple-mountain in Angkor, and that plainness is why it photographs so well. Carving had only just begun when work stopped, so the stepped pyramid has almost no decoration. The result is clean lines, strong shadows and a very solid shape. It was built as the state temple of Jayavarman V, who began it in 975, and it was dedicated around 1000. It was never finished. Five sanctuary towers sit on top of a five-tier pyramid, and the summit stands 21.5 m above the ground. From the phone icon on the map, in the middle of the temple grounds, the pyramid rises above a jungle canopy. The trees make a natural frame around the stone, which works nicely on a phone screen. Late afternoon light brings out the texture of the sandstone. The temple is also shaded after about 1 pm, so morning or late afternoon is kinder than midday. If you want a different view, walk to the southwest corner, try the east side from the approach causeway, or stand on the ground and shoot the full height of the temple with the ultra-wide lens. The four stairways to the top are very steep, so take care and don't rush for a summit shot.
text.geographic_location: Ta Keo stands in the Angkor area. A long causeway, about 500 m, runs east from the temple's eastern entrance to a landing stage on the East Baray.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station stops are listed for this area. Ask for Ta Keo (Prasat Ta Keo) in the Angkor area. Once inside the temple grounds, head for the marked stand-here point; the southwest corner is an optional extra viewpoint. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) at the phone icon on the map to frame the pyramid with the trees. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) from the ground if you want the full height of the temple. Telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) is good for picking out the tops of the towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the pyramid rises above the jungle canopy, and the trees make a natural frame around it. For a second option, walk to the southwest corner, or to the east side to shoot the stepped pyramid from the approach causeway.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the pyramid on one of the upper lines, with a band of treetops below it. Keep the phone level so the stepped sides stay straight. Leave a little sky above the towers. For a quieter alternative to the summit, hold the ultra-wide lens low and tilt up gently to capture the full height.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sunlit stone to set focus, then use the exposure slider to pull the brightness down a little so the sky doesn't wash out. If the pyramid looks too dark against bright sky, try a small boost to the exposure instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the low light picks out the texture in the stone. Morning is also good. The temple is shaded after about 1 pm.

text.access_note: Photography is generally allowed, but it may be restricted in areas under restoration, so check on site for restricted areas.

name: Srah Srang
label: Srah Srang
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Srah Srang' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Srah Srang' (way/568211774): middle (47 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/10930121: large area 'Srah Srang' (917 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Royal bathing pool, lovely at sunrise.

text.description:
Srah Srang, whose name means "Royal Bath", is a large reservoir (a baray) at Angkor, and its western landing terrace is a popular and well-regarded spot for sunrise photos. The reservoir was dug in the mid-10th century. Around the year 1200 Jayavarman VII added the stone landing-stage on its western side. Today the water measures roughly 700 by 350 metres and is still partly flooded. The terrace is cross-shaped. Its steps run down to the water between two guardian lions, and the balustrades along them are carved as nāga serpents, each ending in an upright head with a garuda above it.

This is why it works so well for phone photos. The carved terrace gives you a strong foreground, and the open water behind it gives you a calm, uncluttered background. At sunrise the sun comes up over the trees on the far bank, and on a still morning the sky is mirrored in the water. Stand at the top of the steps, face east and let the stonework frame the view. If you want a change, the shoreline away from the terrace is quieter and more open, and it suits soft reflections of the trees. At sunset the sun goes down between the trees, and in the dry season, when the water is low, a small island stupa can show up as a silhouette. The terrace can get busier in peak season, so arrive before dawn if you want room to choose your spot.
text.geographic_location: Srah Srang is in the Angkor area, south of the East Baray and east of Banteay Kdei. The terrace sits directly across the road from the Banteay Kdei entrance.
text.directions_text: From Siem Reap town, head into the Angkor area; Srah Srang is on the Small Circuit. Once there, look for the Banteay Kdei entrance. The stone terrace and steps are directly across the road, on the western edge of the water. Get there before dawn if you plan to shoot the sunrise. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the terrace, the water and the sky together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the carved balustrades and steps in the foreground. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the sun over the far treeline or the island stupa when the water is low.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Srah Srang (west edge, top of the stone steps down to the jetty, facing east over the water). The reservoir at sunrise with the sun rising over the treetops on the far bank and its reflection in the still water, framed by the naga-balustraded terrace and the guardian lions. At the top of the stone steps down to the jetty, facing east over the water. From here you see the reservoir, the sun rising over the treetops on the far bank and its reflection in the still water. The naga-balustraded terrace and the guardian lions frame the view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line, giving the sky or the reflection most of the frame. Keep a naga balustrade or a lion along one side as a foreground. For an alternative, try the quieter, more open shoreline for a clean reflection of the trees at dawn.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sunrise colours do not wash out. Take a few shots a minute apart as the light changes, and wait for the ripples to settle before you press the shutter. Try a Live Photo to catch moving water or birds.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise, when the sun comes up over the far bank. Sunset is the alternative, with the sun going down between the trees. Check which way the sun is moving on the day you go.

text.access_note: Entry to the Angkor area requires an Angkor Pass, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Facing east from the west-side terrace puts the rising sun ahead of you across the water.
The water is usually calmest early in the morning, which gives the best reflections.
Arriving before dawn gives you more room to choose a spot, as the terrace can get busier at peak season.

name: East Mebon
label: East Mebon
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'ប្រាសាទមេបុណ្យខាងកើត' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/228049177: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'East Mebon temple' (223 m across).
notes: Temple with stone elephants on its corners.

text.description:
East Mebon is a 10th-century temple that once stood on an artificial island in the middle of a huge reservoir, the East Baray. The water has long gone, but the temple still has a stepped, pyramid-like shape, with three tiers, two enclosing walls and a central tower surrounded by four smaller towers at the corners. That layered outline is what makes it work so well on a phone: the steps give you natural lines and levels to build a picture around.

The sculpture is the real draw for close-up photos. Free-standing stone elephants, about two metres high, stand at the corners of the first and second tiers. One guide names the elephant at the southwest corner of the lower tier as the best preserved, so that is the one this spot points you to, while another guide prefers the southeast corner. Both are worth a look if you have time. The temple was dedicated in 953 CE to the Hindu god Shiva and honours the parents of King Rajendravarman. Four landing stages at the base are a reminder that visitors once arrived by boat.

Walk to the southwest corner of the lower tier and stand at the foot of the elephant, then frame it against the stepped base behind. Keep a little distance so the whole animal fits, then move in for a detail shot of the carving. For a second picture, try the temple front when the morning sun reaches the stonework, or a wide view from the upper level over the dry baray with the towers behind. Please don't climb on the statues, and take care on the steep steps.
text.geographic_location: East Mebon sits in the Angkor Archaeological Park, near Siem Reap, in the middle of the now dry East Baray. It lies about 1,200 metres north of Pre Rup.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station stops are relevant here, so travel from Siem Reap town into the Angkor Archaeological Park. East Mebon is about 1,200 metres north of Pre Rup, so if you are already at Pre Rup you are close by. Once at the temple, note that the phone icon on the map marks the middle of the temple. From there, walk to the lower tier and head for the southwest corner, where the elephant stands. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the elephant with the stepped base behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full temple front or the view from the upper level, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for carving details on the towers and lintels.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there, walk to the southwest corner of the lower tier and stand beside the corner elephant. From this corner the photo shows a close-up of the elephant sculpture framed against the temple's stepped base.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the elephant on one of the vertical lines, with the steps rising behind it. Crouch slightly so the animal stands out against the stonework. As an alternative, shoot the temple front when the morning light falls on the carvings, or take a wide view across the dry East Baray with the towers behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the elephant to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the stone keeps its texture. Try portrait mode for a softer background, though the default photo mode often keeps the steps clearer.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise and late afternoon are the recommended times, when low light brings out the texture of the stone.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed site that needs an Angkor Archaeological Park pass, so check the official site before you go.

name: Wat Damnak
label: Wat Damnak
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Wat Damnak' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q107735892: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Active Buddhist pagoda in the town centre.

text.description:
Wat Damnak is a working Buddhist monastery in the city of Siem Reap, and its name recalls its earlier life as a royal home. King Sisowath lived here from 1904 to 1927. After the palace moved, the old courtyard became a pagoda. Today it is one of the city's teaching monasteries, so you may see monks and students about the grounds. In the 1950s the monks added stupas in the courtyard, modelled on Banteay Srei. The Center for Khmer Studies was also set up in the grounds.

For a phone photo, the calmer choice is the lily pond inside the grounds. Colourful water lilies, fish and turtles make a gentle foreground, with the pagoda and trees rising behind the water. It is a quieter picture than the main pagoda front, and it works well if you want something peaceful rather than a straight temple shot. If you also want the classic view, the main pagoda has a traditional Khmer roofline and stone Buddha sculptures, framed by frangipani trees and greenery. Keep your voice down, stay on the paths, and do not point your phone at monks or pupils without asking. Avoid school hours where possible.
text.geographic_location: Wat Damnak lies within the city of Siem Reap, Cambodia, in a monastery compound that also holds a school and the Center for Khmer Studies.
text.directions_text: Wat Damnak is in the city of Siem Reap; use a map app to reach it. Walk into the grounds, then follow the paths to the lily pond within the grounds. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the pond, the lilies and the pagoda behind in one frame. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want to get low and close to the lilies. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the pagoda roof or a single flower without leaning over the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From the water's edge you see the pond with its water lilies and fish in the foreground, and the pagoda and trees behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the water's edge on the lower line, with the pagoda roof on an upper third. Let a few lilies sit in the foreground for depth. For a second picture, walk to the main pagoda and frame its Khmer roofline and stone Buddha sculptures with the frangipani branches and greenery around them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a lily to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white petals keep their detail and the sky is not washed out. Portrait mode can work on a single flower if you stay a short distance away.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the water. Try to avoid school hours where possible.

text.access_note: This is an active monastery and school, so dress modestly, behave respectfully and check the official site before you go for current access rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon light is usually softer on the water.
Modest dress is expected when visiting an active monastery.
Asking permission before photographing monks or pupils is polite.
